title: OLTP vs OLAP
tagline: Transactional speed vs analytical power — row stores, columnar storage, data warehouses, and the ETL pipelines that feed them.

sections.content:
Every database system ever built is ultimately optimized for one of two very different workloads — and the design choices that make it excellent at one make it terrible at the other. **OLTP (Online Transaction Processing)** is the database of the application — the engine that powers every user action. When a customer places an order, a row is inserted into the `orders` table in milliseconds. When a user logs in, their row is fetched by primary key in under a millisecond. When two bank accounts swap money, two rows are updated atomically inside a transaction. OLTP databases are purpose-built for thousands of these tiny, short-lived operations per second.

**OLAP (Online Analytical Processing)** is the database of the analyst. When the CFO wants to know which product categories drove the most revenue growth in Q3 across the Asia-Pacific region, a query might need to scan hundreds of millions of rows, aggregate across multiple dimensions, and return a compact result table. That query could easily run for minutes — which would be catastrophic inside the application database that real users are hitting right now. OLAP systems are built for these long-running, read-heavy, aggregation-intensive workloads.

The same schema design, storage format, indexing strategy, and hardware configuration that makes OLTP blazingly fast makes OLAP painfully slow — and vice versa. This fundamental incompatibility is why nearly every organization beyond a certain scale builds and maintains **separate data infrastructure** for analytics: a **data warehouse** fed by **ETL or ELT pipelines**, powered by **columnar storage engines** with **star schemas** and **partition pruning**. Understanding the distinction between OLTP and OLAP is not merely academic. It determines how you architect systems, where you direct your analytical queries, how much money you spend on infrastructure, and whether your application falls over the next time your data team runs a big report.

This chapter will walk through every layer of the distinction: the physical storage model (row-oriented vs columnar), the schema paradigm (normalized 3NF vs star schema), the pipeline that bridges them (ETL vs ELT), the warehouse optimization techniques (partitioning, clustering, materialized views), and the modern ecosystem of tools — Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, DuckDB, dbt — that have reshaped how organizations handle analytical data.

sections.title: The Shop Counter vs the Accountant's Ledger
sections.content:
OLTP is the shop counter at a busy retail store. Cashiers ring up individual transactions fast, one at a time, returning change to the customer before the next person in line gets impatient. Each transaction is small and self-contained. The register touches only the items being purchased right now. Speed and correctness for individual actions are everything.

OLAP is the accountant sitting in the back office at year-end, running across the complete ledger for the past twelve months. The accountant does not care about individual transactions — they want totals by category, trends by month, anomalies by region. They need to scan every receipt the store ever processed. You would not ask the cashier to run the annual report mid-shift; the line of customers would revolt. Instead you give the accountant a photocopy of the ledger — the data warehouse — so they can crunch numbers without interfering with the checkout line at all.

The photocopy is not perfectly up-to-the-minute (it might be from last night's batch), but the accountant does not need sub-second freshness. They need completeness, historical depth, and aggregation power. These are fundamentally different demands that justify fundamentally different systems.

sections.title: Row-Oriented vs Columnar Storage: The Physical Root of the Difference
sections.content:
The single most important technical distinction between OLTP and OLAP systems is **how data is physically arranged on disk**. Everything else — query performance, compression ratios, indexing strategies, hardware requirements — flows from this one architectural choice.

**Row-oriented storage** (used by PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server) stores all columns of a single row contiguously in a data page. When you read page 47 from the `orders` table, you get the complete record for a set of orders: their IDs, statuses, customer IDs, amounts, timestamps, shipping addresses — all fields, all together. This layout is perfect for OLTP. A query like `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 987654` performs a single B+ tree index lookup, finds the page containing that row, reads the whole row in one disk access. An `INSERT` or `UPDATE` touches exactly the page containing that row.

But consider the analytical query `SELECT SUM(total_amount) FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01'`. In a row store, the database must read every row from every page in the table — even though it only needs the `total_amount` column and the `created_at` column. For a 100 million row orders table with 40 columns, you are reading perhaps 200 GB of data to sum one column. Most of the I/O is wasted.

**Columnar storage** (used by Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, DuckDB, Apache Parquet) stores each column's values contiguously across all rows. All 100 million `total_amount` values are stored together; all 100 million `created_at` values are stored together. The analytical query now reads only the `total_amount` column and the `created_at` column — perhaps 5-10 GB instead of 200 GB. The query engine skips every other column entirely.

**Compression** is the second massive advantage of columnar storage. When values from the same column are stored together, they tend to be similar — a `status` column might contain only the strings `'pending'`, `'shipped'`, and `'delivered'` across all 100 million rows. A dictionary encoding maps those three strings to three integers (0, 1, 2) and stores a sequence of tiny integers. Run-length encoding collapses `'shipped', 'shipped', 'shipped', 'shipped'` into a single `(shipped, 4)` pair. Real columnar systems routinely achieve 5–20x compression ratios compared to row stores on the same data. This further reduces I/O and allows more data to fit in memory.

The tradeoff: reading or writing a single complete row in a columnar store is slow, because the row's fields are scattered across many separate column files. OLTP operations that touch complete rows (the dominant pattern) are inherently slower. This is why you never run your application against a columnar warehouse.

sections.title: OLTP Schema Design: Third Normal Form and Why It Matters
sections.content:
OLTP databases are typically designed in **Third Normal Form (3NF)** or close to it. Normalization eliminates data redundancy by breaking data into many small related tables. An e-commerce database might have separate tables for `customers`, `addresses`, `orders`, `order_items`, `products`, `product_categories`, `inventory`, `payments`, and `shipments`. Data is stored in exactly one place; every other table references it by foreign key.

**Why normalization is right for OLTP:** When a customer changes their shipping address, you update exactly one row in the `addresses` table. There is no risk of updating it in some places but not others (an **update anomaly**). When you insert a new order, you do not duplicate the customer's name, email, and address — you just store their `customer_id`. Storage is minimized. Consistency is easy to maintain with foreign key constraints.

**Why normalization is wrong for OLAP:** An analytical query answering 'total revenue by customer region by product category for the past year' in a 3NF schema might require joining six or more tables. The query optimizer must process millions of intermediate join rows. The unpredictable join shapes make optimization difficult. Each query looks different, requiring manual tuning. Performance is inconsistent and often poor on large datasets.

OLTP normalization is designed to minimize write anomalies and storage. These are simply not the primary concerns in a read-only analytical system.

sections.title: Star Schema: The OLAP Schema Paradigm
sections.content:
Data warehouses use a fundamentally different schema design called the **star schema** (or its variant, the **snowflake schema**). A star schema has two types of tables: one central **fact table** and several surrounding **dimension tables**. The relationship looks like a star when drawn, hence the name.

**The fact table** contains rows that represent measurable business events: an order placed, a page view, a payment received, a product shipped. Each row stores quantitative metrics (revenue, quantity, duration, count) and foreign keys pointing to dimension tables. The fact table is by far the largest table — potentially billions of rows — and is the primary target for aggregation queries.

**Dimension tables** store descriptive attributes that give context to the facts: who (customer dimension: name, email, city, region, segment), what (product dimension: name, category, subcategory, brand, price), when (date dimension: date, day of week, week, month, quarter, year, is_holiday, fiscal_period), and where (geography dimension: city, state, country, region). Dimension tables are small relative to the fact table — a date dimension for a decade is only 3,650 rows.

**Why star schema works for OLAP:** All analytical questions are answered by joining the fact table to one or more dimension tables and aggregating. The join pattern is always the same — fact to dim, never dim to dim. This predictability lets the query optimizer build efficient execution plans. Dimension data is denormalized (the customer's city and region are stored directly on the customer row rather than in a separate `cities` table), eliminating the multi-hop joins that slow down normalized schemas. The optimizer can push filters down to dimension tables first (reducing the fact rows to join), then aggregate — a very efficient execution pattern.

**Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCDs):** Dimension values change over time. A customer might move cities; a product might change category. How you handle this determines whether historical analysis is accurate. **SCD Type 1** simply overwrites — the new value replaces the old, losing history. **SCD Type 2** adds a new row for the new version, with `valid_from` and `valid_to` timestamps and an `is_current` flag, preserving complete history. Most production warehouses use Type 2 for important dimensions like customers and products.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
-- OLTP: fast single-row lookup (row store, B+ tree index seek)
-- Executes in < 1 ms via index on orders.id
SELECT id, status, total_amount, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE id = 987654;

-- OLAP: aggregate over billions of rows (columnar warehouse)
-- Run in BigQuery / Snowflake / DuckDB
-- Columnar storage reads ONLY revenue and date_id bytes from fact table
SELECT
  d.year,
  d.quarter,
  c.region,
  p.category,
  SUM(f.revenue)      AS total_revenue,
  COUNT(f.order_id)   AS order_count,
  AVG(f.revenue)      AS avg_order_value
FROM fact_orders      AS f
JOIN dim_dates        AS d  ON f.date_id     = d.date_id
JOIN dim_customers    AS c  ON f.customer_id  = c.customer_id
JOIN dim_products     AS p  ON f.product_id   = p.product_id
WHERE d.year = 2024
  AND c.region IN ('APAC', 'EMEA')
GROUP BY d.year, d.quarter, c.region, p.category
ORDER BY d.quarter, total_revenue DESC;

-- Partitioning + clustering setup (Snowflake example)
-- Partition pruning ensures only 2024 micro-partitions are scanned
ALTER TABLE fact_orders CLUSTER BY (year, region);

-- BigQuery equivalent: partition by date column
-- CREATE TABLE fact_orders
--   PARTITION BY DATE_TRUNC(order_date, MONTH)
--   CLUSTER BY region, product_category
-- AS SELECT ...
sections.explanation: The OLTP query is a point lookup — one index seek, one page read, negligible I/O regardless of table size. The OLAP query scans hundreds of millions of fact rows, but columnar storage means only the `revenue`, `order_id`, `date_id`, `customer_id`, and `product_id` columns are read. The warehouse then applies partition pruning to skip non-2024 data before even scanning. Clustering by `(year, region)` further enables block-level pruning within partitions.

sections.title: ETL vs ELT: The Pipelines That Bridge OLTP and OLAP
sections.content:
Data does not teleport from your application database into the warehouse. A pipeline must extract it, possibly transform it, and load it. Two architectural patterns dominate: **ETL (Extract, Transform, Load)** and **ELT (Extract, Load, Transform)**.

**ETL** emerged in the era when data warehouses were expensive on-premise appliances with limited compute. The pipeline runs on a separate processing server: extract raw data from source systems, transform it (clean, join, reshape, aggregate) using code (Python, Spark, Informatica), and then load only the clean, final data into the warehouse. Transformation happens outside the warehouse. Traditional tools: Informatica PowerCenter, IBM DataStage, Talend, Apache Spark jobs.

**ELT** flips the order. Raw data is loaded directly into the warehouse first, then transformed inside the warehouse using SQL. This became practical with cloud warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) that provide virtually unlimited elastic compute on demand. Transforming inside the warehouse is often faster (the engine has already loaded the data into memory for querying) and simpler (SQL instead of distributed Spark jobs). The dominant ELT tool today is **dbt (data build tool)**, which lets analysts write SQL SELECT statements that dbt compiles into CREATE TABLE AS or CREATE VIEW statements, runs inside the warehouse, and version-controls as code.

**Why ELT won for cloud warehouses:** compute in Snowflake or BigQuery is cheap and elastic. You do not need to size a separate Spark cluster. Transformations are version-controlled SQL files checked into git. Non-engineers can write and modify transformations. dbt handles dependency ordering (model A must run before model B that references it), testing (assert that `customer_id` is never null), documentation, and incremental materialization.

**Batch vs streaming:** Both ETL and ELT are traditionally batch processes — run every hour, or every night. **Streaming ELT** (Kafka + Flink, or services like Fivetran and Airbyte with near-real-time connectors) reduces latency to seconds or minutes. Streaming is harder to implement but essential when the business needs near-real-time dashboards — for example, a fraud detection dashboard that must reflect transactions from the last 60 seconds.

flowchart LR
  A["Source: OLTP DB"] --> B["EXTRACT"]
  B --> C{"ETL or ELT?"}
  C -->|"ETL"| D["TRANSFORM\noutside warehouse\nSpark / Python"]
  D --> E["LOAD clean data\ninto warehouse"]
  C -->|"ELT"| F["LOAD raw data\ninto warehouse"]

sections.caption: ETL transforms outside the warehouse before loading. ELT loads raw data first then transforms using the warehouse's own compute — dominant pattern with cloud warehouses.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
-- dbt model: models/marts/revenue_by_region.sql
-- ELT transform that runs INSIDE the warehouse
-- dbt compiles this SELECT into CREATE TABLE AS SELECT

-- {{ config(
--   materialized = 'table',
--   partition_by = { 'field': 'order_year', 'data_type': 'int64' },
--   cluster_by  = ['region', 'category']
-- ) }}

SELECT
  d.year                        AS order_year,
  d.quarter                     AS order_quarter,
  c.region,
  p.category,
  SUM(f.revenue)                AS total_revenue,
  COUNT(DISTINCT f.customer_id) AS unique_customers,
  COUNT(f.order_id)             AS total_orders
FROM {{ ref('fact_orders') }}     AS f
JOIN {{ ref('dim_dates') }}       AS d USING (date_id)
JOIN {{ ref('dim_customers') }}   AS c USING (customer_id)
JOIN {{ ref('dim_products') }}    AS p USING (product_id)
WHERE f.is_test_order = FALSE
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4

-- dbt test: schema.yml
-- models:
--   - name: revenue_by_region
--     columns:
--       - name: total_revenue
--         tests:
--           - not_null
--           - dbt_utils.accepted_range:
--               min_value: 0

-- Incremental model pattern (only process new rows each run)
-- {{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='order_id') }}
-- {% if is_incremental() %}
--   WHERE f.created_at > (SELECT MAX(created_at) FROM {{ this }})
-- {% endif %}
sections.explanation: dbt models are plain SQL SELECT statements. The `{{ ref() }}` macro creates a dependency graph — dbt runs models in topological order. The `config()` block sets materialization strategy (table, view, incremental, ephemeral), partitioning, and clustering. Incremental models only process rows added since the last run, making large tables feasible without full rebuilds.

sections.title: Warehouse Optimization: Partitioning, Clustering, and Materialized Views
sections.content:
A naive columnar warehouse still performs poorly at petabyte scale without further optimization. Three techniques are essential: **partitioning**, **clustering**, and **materialized views**.

**Partitioning** divides a table into discrete physical segments called partitions, each containing a subset of rows. The partition key is almost always a time column: `order_date`, `event_timestamp`, `created_at`. Snowflake automatically creates **micro-partitions** (16–512 MB compressed) and tracks the min/max of every column in each micro-partition in its metadata layer. When a query includes `WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01'`, Snowflake consults the metadata, identifies which micro-partitions could contain 2024 rows, and skips all others. This is **partition pruning** — reducing a full table scan of 10 years of data to a scan of just the 2024 partitions. The savings are multiplicative: 10x data reduction means 10x less I/O, 10x less compute, 10x lower cost, 10x faster results.

**Clustering** (Snowflake) and **table clustering** (BigQuery) further sort data within partitions by additional columns. If queries commonly filter by `region = 'APAC'` and `product_category = 'Electronics'`, clustering by those columns packs APAC Electronics rows into nearby micro-partitions. The engine can skip non-matching clusters without scanning them. Think of it as a coarser-grained index at the storage level.

**Materialized views** (also called **pre-aggregated tables** or **aggregate tables** in some systems) pre-compute expensive aggregations and store the results physically. A materialized view for `SELECT year, region, SUM(revenue) FROM fact_orders GROUP BY 1, 2` computes once and stores. Subsequent queries against this view read hundreds of rows instead of hundreds of millions. dbt calls these **mart models** or **aggregate models**. The tradeoff: materialized views go stale and must be refreshed, adding maintenance complexity. Most systems support automatic incremental refresh — updating only the partitions where source data changed.

**Query result caching** is another free optimization in cloud warehouses. Snowflake and BigQuery both cache query results for 24 hours (Snowflake) or indefinitely (BigQuery for unchanged data). An identical query run twice returns instantly from cache at zero compute cost. Dashboards that refresh every 5 minutes effectively pay for compute once per 24 hours if the underlying data has not changed.

sections.title: The Modern Warehouse Ecosystem: Tools and When to Use Them
sections.content:
Understanding the landscape of tools helps you make architectural decisions — not just pass interviews.

**Snowflake** pioneered the separation of storage and compute in a cloud warehouse. Storage (in S3 or Azure Blob) is billed separately from compute clusters (Virtual Warehouses). You can spin up 20 separate Virtual Warehouses hitting the same storage — isolation between the data team, the ML team, and the embedded analytics team, with no resource contention. Snowflake auto-suspends idle warehouses and auto-scales under load. Its Time Travel feature lets you query the state of any table at any point in the past 90 days. Its data sharing feature allows sharing live data across accounts with zero-copy cloning.

**BigQuery** (Google Cloud) is serverless — there are no clusters to provision or size. You submit a query and Google dynamically allocates hundreds of slots (units of compute) behind the scenes. Billing is per byte scanned (or flat-rate for predictable workloads). BigQuery's strengths are its integration with the Google ecosystem (Looker, Vertex AI, Pub/Sub) and its ML capabilities (BigQuery ML allows training models in SQL). Its weakness is less control over query execution and sometimes surprising cost at high scan volumes.

**Amazon Redshift** is the oldest major cloud warehouse. Originally it required sizing clusters (node type and count) manually. Redshift Serverless (launched 2022) now offers a BigQuery-style serverless option. Redshift excels in AWS-native architectures and has strong Redshift Spectrum for querying S3 data lakes directly.

**DuckDB** is the emerging wildcard: an in-process columnar analytical database that runs inside a Python script, a dbt project, or a Node.js application. There are no servers. DuckDB can query Parquet files on S3 directly and perform TPC-H benchmarks at multi-gigabyte scale on a laptop. It is replacing Pandas for medium-scale data transformations and powering a new generation of lightweight analytical tools.

**Apache Parquet** is the de facto columnar file format for data lakes. Parquet files are columnar, compressed (Snappy or Zstandard), and schema-aware. They can be read by Spark, DuckDB, BigQuery, Athena, Redshift Spectrum, Trino, and dozens of other tools. If you are building a data lake or exchanging analytical data between systems, Parquet is almost always the right format.

**dbt (data build tool)** is the transformation layer gluing everything together. It treats SQL transformations as software: version-controlled, tested, documented, with a dependency DAG. Teams write dbt models as SQL SELECT statements; dbt compiles and runs them in the warehouse. dbt Cloud adds a scheduler, IDE, and lineage graph. dbt has become the standard for ELT transformations across all major warehouses.

sections.title: Edge Cases, Misconceptions, and the HTAP Middle Ground
sections.content:
**Common misconception: 'just use a read replica for analytics.'** Many teams start by pointing analytical queries at a PostgreSQL read replica to avoid hurting the primary. This works at small scale but fails as data grows. Read replicas are still row-oriented — the full-scan I/O problem remains. Replication lag means the replica may be seconds to minutes behind, causing confusing query results. And a long-running analytical query still starves other read queries on the replica. Read replicas buy time; they do not solve the fundamental architectural mismatch.

**HTAP (Hybrid Transactional/Analytical Processing)** is the category of systems attempting to serve both workloads from one engine. TiDB (by PingCAP) and SingleStore (formerly MemSQL) are notable examples. They maintain a row-oriented store for transactions and a columnar store for analytics, with automatic replication between them. HTAP is powerful but complex, and most organizations with serious analytical needs eventually find that a purpose-built warehouse outperforms the HTAP hybrid at large scale.

**Lakehouse architecture** (popularized by Databricks with Delta Lake, and now also with Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi) blurs the line between data lake and warehouse. Raw data lands in cloud object storage (S3) in open columnar formats. A transactional metadata layer (Delta Lake, Iceberg) adds ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel, and incremental processing on top of those files. Query engines like Trino, Spark, and Databricks SQL can then run warehouse-grade queries directly on the lake. The lakehouse reduces the need to copy data from a lake into a separate warehouse, simplifying the architecture and reducing cost.

**When OLAP freshness matters:** Traditional batch ETL produces data that is 24 hours stale. For financial dashboards, executive reporting, and long-term trend analysis, this is acceptable. For operational dashboards (monitoring delivery driver locations, tracking live campaign performance, watching order volumes in real-time), 24-hour lag is not. Streaming pipelines (Kafka + Flink, or Fivetran with CDC connectors) reduce latency to seconds but significantly increase architectural complexity. Most organizations settle on a hybrid: streaming for operational metrics, batch for deep historical analysis.

**Historical context:** The terms OLTP and OLAP were coined by E.F. Codd (inventor of the relational model) in 1985 and 1993 respectively. The first columnar database was Sybase IQ, introduced in 1994. Amazon Redshift (2012) brought columnar warehousing to the cloud masses. Snowflake's storage/compute separation (2014) and Google BigQuery's serverless model transformed the economics. The modern explosion of the 'modern data stack' — Fivetran + Snowflake + dbt + Looker — emerged between 2015 and 2020 and is now the dominant architecture at growth-stage and enterprise companies.

**Interview and production traps to know:** Never run heavy aggregation queries on your OLTP production database — even a `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders` on 100 M rows can run for minutes, holding locks and starving application queries. If you must query OLTP for analytics, use a read replica and set a statement timeout. In warehouse queries, always filter on the partition key (usually the date column) — omitting it triggers a full table scan costing dollars in BigQuery. In Snowflake, use `EXPLAIN` to verify partition pruning is happening; look for 'partitions scanned' vs 'partitions total' in the query profile. In dbt, prefer incremental models over full table rebuilds for fact tables larger than ~10 M rows — rebuilding 10 B rows every night is expensive and unnecessary when only today's rows changed.

items: **OLTP** (Online Transaction Processing) optimizes for low-latency reads and writes of individual rows; row-oriented storage excels here by colocating all fields of each row for fast complete-record access.

**OLAP** (Online Analytical Processing) optimizes for scanning and aggregating millions to billions of rows; **columnar storage** excels by reading only the queried columns from disk and compressing similar column values 5–20x.

**Star schema** (fact table + dimension tables) is the OLAP schema paradigm — it denormalizes data into predictable, optimizer-friendly join patterns, replacing the multi-hop joins of normalized 3NF schemas.
**ETL** transforms data before loading into the warehouse; **ELT** loads raw data first then transforms inside the warehouse using SQL — ELT with dbt is now the dominant pattern for cloud warehouses.
**Partition pruning** skips irrelevant partitions at query time; **clustering** further narrows scans within partitions — together they can reduce data scanned by 99%+ for well-filtered queries.
**Modern tools**: Snowflake (storage/compute separation), BigQuery (serverless), DuckDB (in-process), Parquet (file format), and dbt (ELT transforms) form the backbone of the modern data stack.

**The fundamental rule**: never run heavy analytical queries on your OLTP production database. Route analytics to a dedicated warehouse, read replica, or columnar extension — the architectural separation exists to protect both workloads.

quiz.question: Which system is better suited for a query that sums revenue across 500 million orders?
options: OLTP row-store database like PostgreSQL
OLAP columnar warehouse like Snowflake
A key-value store like Redis
A document database like MongoDB
quiz.explanation: OLAP columnar warehouses like Snowflake read only the revenue column from disk, skipping all other columns entirely. This makes full-scan aggregations 10–100x faster than row-stores, which must read complete rows even when only one column is needed.

quiz.question: Why does columnar storage compress better than row-oriented storage?
options: Columns use smaller data types than rows
Adjacent values in a column are similar, making encodings like run-length and dictionary encoding very effective
Columnar storage omits NULL values entirely from disk
Columnar storage uses GZIP by default while row stores do not
quiz.explanation: A column stores the same field for millions of rows consecutively. Similar values — for example a status column containing only 'pending', 'shipped', and 'delivered' — compress dramatically with dictionary encoding or run-length encoding. Row-oriented pages mix many different field types, reducing compression effectiveness.

quiz.question: In a star schema, the fact table contains:
options: Descriptive attributes like customer name and product category
Numeric metrics and foreign keys to dimension tables
The schema definitions of all other warehouse tables
Only slowly changing dimension history
quiz.explanation: The fact table stores measurable business events (revenue, quantity, clicks) along with foreign keys pointing to dimension tables. It is the largest table, often billions of rows, and is the primary target for aggregation queries.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between ETL and ELT?
options: ETL uses SQL; ELT always uses Python or Spark
ETL transforms data before loading into the warehouse; ELT loads raw data first then transforms inside the warehouse
ETL is always batch; ELT is always streaming
ETL is used only for OLTP; ELT is used only for OLAP migration
quiz.explanation: ETL transforms data in a separate processing layer (Spark, Informatica) before loading the final data into the warehouse. ELT loads raw data into the warehouse first, then transforms it with SQL using the warehouse's own compute — the pattern popularized by dbt with cloud warehouses.

quiz.question: What is 'partition pruning' in a data warehouse?
options: Dropping old partitions to reclaim storage space
Skipping partitions whose min/max range cannot contain rows matching the query filter
Merging small partitions into larger ones for efficiency
Reindexing partition columns to speed up lookups
quiz.explanation: Partition pruning means the query engine inspects partition metadata (min/max values) and skips all partitions that cannot contain rows matching the filter. For a date-partitioned table with a WHERE year = 2024 filter, all other year partitions are skipped entirely — reducing I/O proportionally to the fraction of data filtered out.

quiz.question: A normalized OLTP schema with six tables performs poorly in a data warehouse. The standard fix is:
options: Add more indexes to every table in the normalized schema
Denormalize into a star or snowflake schema with a central fact table
Run the analytical queries on the OLTP primary server with a long timeout
Partition every table by its primary key column
quiz.explanation: Warehouses denormalize data into a star schema — fact tables with foreign keys to flattened dimension tables. This replaces unpredictable multi-hop joins with a consistent fact-to-dim join pattern that columnar engines and optimizers handle very efficiently.

quiz.question: Which tool is most closely associated with ELT transformations inside a cloud data warehouse?
options: Apache Spark
dbt (data build tool)
Informatica PowerCenter
Apache Sqoop
quiz.explanation: dbt (data build tool) lets analysts write SQL SELECT statements that dbt compiles into CREATE TABLE AS or CREATE VIEW statements inside the warehouse. It popularized ELT by treating SQL transforms as version-controlled, tested, documented code — now the industry standard for warehouse transformations.

quiz.question: Why should heavy analytical queries NOT be run on the OLTP production database?
options: OLTP databases cannot parse GROUP BY and aggregation functions
Analytical full-table scans hold locks, spike I/O load, and starve time-sensitive application queries
OLTP databases do not support joins across multiple tables
Analytical queries require column-level permissions unavailable in OLTP engines
quiz.explanation: Full table scans for analytics can run for minutes, holding shared locks and consuming I/O and CPU that application queries need for sub-millisecond response times. This causes latency spikes for end users and can trigger cascading failures in the application.

quiz.question: What is the primary advantage of Snowflake's separation of storage and compute?
options: Queries are automatically converted from SQL to columnar format
Multiple independent compute clusters can query the same data simultaneously without resource contention
Storage is automatically backed up every minute at no extra cost
Snowflake automatically normalizes data into third normal form
quiz.explanation: Because storage (in S3/Azure Blob) is decoupled from compute (Virtual Warehouses), you can spin up 20 separate Virtual Warehouses all reading the same data — giving the data team, ML team, and analytics team isolated compute that scales independently without competing for the same resources.

quiz.question: A row-oriented database must read a full 8 KB page to access one column value. A columnar store avoids this because:
options: Columnar stores use smaller page sizes of 512 bytes
All values for a single column are stored contiguously, so reading that column reads only its bytes from disk
Columnar stores keep all columns in memory and never read from disk
Columnar stores compress each row individually so only one row is decompressed at a time
quiz.explanation: Columnar storage places all values for column C contiguously on disk. A query needing only column C reads only C's storage footprint — skipping bytes for every other column. For a 40-column table, this can reduce I/O by 95%+ for single-column aggregations like SUM(revenue).
